transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you for seeing me. Well, I decided to make an appointment because... I mean, I've been a graphic designer for a long time, right? I got my bachelor's years ago, and I'm 40 now, so I've been in the industry long enough to know my job inside and out. But lately, I keep getting these... these really nagging thoughts. It's so frustrating. 

I’ll be working on a layout, and I just get this intense feeling that I’ve missed some tiny, microscopic mistake somewhere. A typo, or a misalignment, something like that. Or, even worse, I'll email a proof to a client, and my brain immediately starts telling me I sent the wrong version. You know how in design you always end up with files named 'final' and then 'final_final_v2'? Well, I'll start thinking I sent the messy draft instead of the approved final. 

And the thing is, even when I can see it’s probably fine—like, logically I know I clicked the right attachment and I know my work is solid—my mind just keeps circling back to it. It just loops and loops. I'll be driving home or trying to relax and watch a show, and I just can't stop thinking about that layout or that email, wondering if I ruined the whole project. It's just taking up so much mental energy, and I really don't know how to turn it off, which is why I thought I should finally talk to someone about it.
Are these thoughts and worries affecting your ability to do everyday things or enjoy activities you normally like?

Well, I mean... yes and no, I guess? Like, I am still getting my work done, ultimately. The clients are getting their deliverables, so from the outside, maybe it looks fine. But day-to-day, especially at the office... it’s definitely taking a toll on how I function. 

For instance, we have these internal deadlines, right? Like milestones where the account managers or the rest of the team reviews the drafts before anything goes out. And lately, I’ve actually started missing those internal deadlines. Which is just *so* unlike me. But I just sit there staring at the screen, zooming in to 400% on a graphic, just completely paralyzed that I've messed up the kerning or left a layer hidden or something stupid. So I end up submitting things late to my own team because I just can't let the file go.

And... well, it’s also really affecting the actual work I do, which used to be the part I enjoyed the most. I’ve always been known for pitching really out-of-the-box, bolder design ideas. You know, complex layering, experimental typography, that sort of thing. But recently? I find myself just holding back. I’ll come up with a great concept, and then my brain just goes, "No, that’s too complicated, there are too many moving parts, you’re definitely going to overlook a mistake if you do that." So I end up watering it down and just submitting these really safe, standard, almost boring layouts. 

And that’s what really scares me, honestly. Because, like I said, I’m 40. I’ve been doing this a long time, and I am really, really trying to position myself for a creative director role. I've been working toward that for years. But if I’m missing internal deadlines and just constantly playing it safe because I’m so afraid of making a mistake... I mean, I’m terrified I’m going to completely damage my chances of getting that promotion. You don't make creative director by being safe and slow, you know? You have to be innovative. So it's just... it's really getting in my own way and sucking the joy out of the design process, even though I'm technically still finishing the projects.
Do you ever find yourself repeating certain actions or checks, like re-emailing a file or re-checking your work multiple times, in an attempt to alleviate these worries about mistakes?

Yeah, I do. I mean, it’s not like I’m spending eight hours straight doing it, but it’s definitely a whole routine now that I never used to have. 

Like, before I submit a piece of work—let’s say it’s a brochure layout or something—I used to just finish it, hit save, and send it off. But now? Now I have to go back and re-open the file. And then I’ll literally sit there and compare every single layer. I’ll turn the visibility of the layers on and off, on and off, just to make absolutely sure nothing shifted or got hidden by accident. And then I’ll re-save it. Sometimes I’ll re-save it two or three times, just watching the little progress bar to make sure the computer actually processed the save command correctly, because what if it glitched, right? 

And it’s not just the clicking and saving, either. I also do this thing where I have to mentally walk through every single design choice I made, one more time, before I can let it go. Like, I’ll sit there staring at the screen and I’ll tell myself, "Okay, I used Helvetica for the header because the brand guidelines say so, I set the tracking to 50 because it looked too tight, I aligned the logo to the right margin..." I just go through this whole mental checklist. 

And, you know, it doesn’t take over my *entire* day. It’s not like I’m trapped at my desk until midnight doing this. But it does make me so much slower. Every project takes longer than it should because of this whole song and dance I have to do at the end. And like I was saying before, it just makes me feel so much less free creatively. Because when I know I’m going to have to do this whole exhausting review process at the end, I just don't want to make complex design choices. The more layers I have, the more things I have to check, so I just keep it simple to save myself the headache. It’s just so frustrating because I *know* I don't need to do all this, but if I don't, I just feel this horrible knot in my stomach that I missed something.
Do you experience any physical sensations, like a racing heart or tightness in your chest, when these worries about mistakes come up?

Physical sensations... like a racing heart? Um, no, not really. I mean, I know some people get that, where they feel like they can't breathe or their chest gets all tight when they're stressed about work, but for me, it's not really a physical thing like that at all. It's pretty much entirely in my head. 

Well, I did mention that knot in my stomach earlier, but honestly, even that isn't a real, sharp physical pain or anything, you know? It's more just a... a heavy sense of mental dread. My heart doesn't start pounding out of my chest when I'm staring at the layers panel in Illustrator, wondering if I accidentally hid the wrong text box. I'll literally be sitting perfectly still at my desk in my ergonomic chair, breathing totally normally, probably sipping my iced coffee, but inside my head, it's just this incredibly loud, looping track of 'you missed a typo, you sent the wrong file, the client is going to notice.' 

So, physically, I feel completely fine. There's no sweating, no shaking, no chest tightness at all. I just feel... tired. Like, really, really mentally drained from all the overthinking. By the time I actually hit send on a final proof to an account manager, my body is perfectly calm, but my brain feels like it just ran an absolute marathon. I've always been pretty physically resilient, even when agency life gets crazy with huge campaigns and tight turnarounds, so I don't really get those physical stress reactions. It's just this very specific, exhausting mental loop.
Are these worries and repeated checks affecting your relationships with colleagues or friends outside of work?

Um, no, actually. Not at all, which I guess is a silver lining? 

I mean, with my colleagues... sure, I’m missing those internal deadlines like I said, but they don't really know *why*. Like, I work really closely with this one account manager, Sarah, on our biggest tech client, and she just thinks I’m being my usual meticulous self. In the agency world, being a perfectionist is almost worn like a badge of honor, right? So they don’t see the panicked checking, they just see me taking extra time to tweak a layout. We still grab coffee, we still joke around on Slack all day about whatever shows we're watching. Nobody is mad at me or avoiding me or anything, they just think I'm deep in the zone. 

And as for my friends outside of work? Oh, they have absolutely no idea. I’m very good at compartmentalizing that part of my life, I think. When I leave the office—or, well, close my laptop if I'm working from home—I don't really bring that specific panic with me. My friends and I have this standing brunch every other Sunday, and we mostly just talk about their kids, or dating, or whatever drama is happening in their lives. I don't sit there at the restaurant worrying about whether I left a layer hidden on a brochure from Friday afternoon. The worry is just so specifically tied to the actual act of designing and staring at the software and sending the deliverables. 

So if I'm out at dinner, I'm just out at dinner. I mean, occasionally I might vent to them about work being stressful, but who doesn't do that? It's never about the checking or the mental lists. So yeah, my social life and my work relationships are completely intact, thankfully. I just kind of keep all the exhausting stuff completely bottled up in my own head while I'm sitting at my desk.
Are you having trouble sleeping at night due to these worries about mistakes?

Sleep? Oh, no, my sleep is actually totally fine. I mean, I know a lot of people who get stressed at work end up lying awake at 3:00 AM staring at the ceiling, thinking about an email they sent or worrying about a presentation, but I don't really do that. 

It’s kind of like what I was saying about my friends and social life—I’m pretty good at leaving the work panic at work. Once I finally get through my whole checking routine and shut my laptop down for the night, it’s like a switch flips. The anxiety is so tied to the actual files and the software and the act of sending things off. So when I'm in my bedroom, in my pajamas, reading a book or watching TV, the files aren't in front of me anymore, so the immediate threat—or whatever you want to call it—is just gone. 

I usually try to wind down with a cup of chamomile tea—I know, it’s such a cliché, but it really works for me—and maybe read a chapter or two of whatever novel I’m into at the moment. Right now it's this historical fiction thing set in the 1920s, very atmospheric. And then I just turn out the light and I’m usually out within ten or fifteen minutes. I sleep a solid seven or eight hours, which I know is a luxury for a lot of people my age, especially in my industry. 

So yeah, I don't have those racing thoughts when my head hits the pillow. I'm not mentally reviewing my font choices or worrying about hidden layers while I'm trying to sleep. The exhaustion I feel is just from the mental marathon during the day, so by the time I go to bed, my brain is honestly just ready to shut down. I guess I'm really lucky in that regard, because if I wasn't sleeping on top of all this daytime stress, I think I'd be in much worse shape. But no, the nights are perfectly peaceful. It's just the hours between 9 and 5 that are the problem.
Are you feeling like these worries and checks are significantly affecting your overall happiness or sense of fulfillment outside of your specific work tasks?

Happiness and fulfillment outside of work? Um, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say they're affecting my overall happiness at all, really. 

Like I was saying before about compartmentalizing, it really does just stay at the office. Or, well, at my desk, since I do work from home a couple of days a week now. But you know what I mean. My life outside of work is actually really good! I have my friends, I have my brunch Sundays, I love my apartment—I just redecorated my living room, actually, kind of a mid-century modern vibe with lots of plants, which has been such a fun project. I spend a lot of time on the weekends just propagating my pothos and finding vintage planters at flea markets. It's so relaxing and fulfilling, and I never, ever think about work or worry about making a mistake when I'm doing that. 

I guess you could say my life is very split right down the middle. There's the work me, who is constantly checking and re-checking and feeling totally drained by 5 PM, and then there's the weekend me, who is perfectly happy, fulfilled, and honestly just living a very normal, pleasant life. I still love going to art museums, I still love trying new restaurants in the city... none of that has changed or been ruined by what's happening at work. 

I think because my symptoms—or, whatever you want to call this checking thing—are so specifically tied to Adobe Creative Suite and client deliverables, it just doesn't bleed into my personal joy. If I'm painting on a canvas for fun on a Saturday, there's no "undo" button, there's no layers panel, there's no client who is going to yell at me if the color is slightly off. So I don't feel that panic. I just feel creative and happy. 

So, yeah, I'm very thankful that it hasn't taken over my whole life. It's just a very frustrating, exhausting thing I have to deal with during business hours. But once I log off, I really do feel like myself again. I can still enjoy my life and feel fulfilled by all my hobbies and relationships. It's just... I wish the work part wasn't so hard, you know? But overall happiness? Yeah, that's still very much intact.
Do you feel like these worries and checks are significantly interfering with your ability to enjoy or perform daily activities outside of work?

Um, outside of work? No, not at all. Like I was saying with my weekend routine and my apartment, I can do all my normal daily stuff without a hitch. Going to the grocery store, doing my laundry, cooking dinner, taking care of my plants—none of that is affected in the slightest. I don't have any issues functioning when I'm just living my life. 

But... well, it's really just the job where it's taking a toll, and it's starting to take a pretty big one. I mean, I *am* still getting my work done, ultimately. The clients are getting their final files, and the agency is getting paid. But it's the process that's completely bogged down. I’ve started missing those internal deadlines I mentioned earlier. Like, if Sarah needs a rough draft by Tuesday morning so she can review it before we present to the client on Thursday, I'll end up pushing it to Wednesday afternoon because I'm just stuck in that endless loop of checking the bleed margins and the font kerning over and over again. She's been understanding so far, but it's definitely not a good look for me.

And honestly, what really breaks my heart—and I've been thinking about this a lot lately, especially since I recently turned 40 and you just naturally start evaluating where you are in your career—is that I'm holding back on my actual designs. I used to be known for these really bold, complex, out-of-the-box layouts. But lately? I'm just pitching these very safe, minimal, almost boring concepts. Because in my head, a simpler design means fewer layers in Photoshop, fewer clipping masks, fewer elements that I have to obsessively check before I export the file. I'm literally dumbing down my own creative work because I'm so terrified I’ll overlook something in a more complicated file and make a fool of myself. 

And that's a huge problem for me, because my goal has always been to move toward a creative director role. I want to be the one leading the creative vision for these campaigns. But how can I ask for that promotion, or how can I even build the portfolio I need to prove I deserve it, when I'm too paralyzed to pitch a bold idea? I feel like I'm quietly sabotaging my own career trajectory just to avoid the panic of checking a complex file. So, even though I can go out to brunch or paint on a Saturday just fine... this whole thing is really damaging my chances of moving up in the agency, and that's incredibly frustrating to realize.
Do you feel like these worries and checks are causing you a lot of emotional pain or distress?

Emotional pain? Um, no, I wouldn't really use those words. Distress is probably a bit too strong of a word, too. 

I mean, when I think of emotional pain, I think of... well, like when my long-term boyfriend and I broke up back when I was 34. That was pain, you know? I was crying all the time, I couldn't eat, I just had this deep, heavy ache in my chest for months. This isn't like that at all. It's not a deep sadness or anything that makes me want to break down and cry. 

It’s really more just... intensely annoying? Like, it's a massive inconvenience. It's frustrating, especially like I was just saying about my career trajectory, because I know I'm getting in my own way and that bothers me on a logical level. But I don't feel emotionally devastated by it. 

Sometimes I think about it like having a really, really bad commute. Like, imagine if you had to sit in gridlock traffic for two hours every single day just to get to a job you otherwise completely love. You don't feel emotional pain about the traffic, you just feel drained and irritated by the time you get there. You get home and you're like, "Ugh, I can't believe I wasted so much time staring at somebody's bumper." That's exactly how I feel when I finally close out of Illustrator after checking the bleed lines and the hex codes for the twentieth time. I'm just annoyed with myself. I'll sit back in my desk chair and just let out this big, heavy sigh, like, "Why do I have to do this?" 

So, no, I wouldn't call it pain. And "distress" sounds so... I don't know, almost dramatic? Like someone who is having a total breakdown. I'm definitely not having a breakdown. I'm just incredibly fed up with my own brain between the hours of nine and five. It’s tedious. It’s like doing your taxes every single day. You hate it, it completely drains your battery, but it doesn't break your heart. I just really want the cycle to stop so I can get back to being the bold designer I used to be, and so I don't have to waste so much energy. But emotionally? Honestly, I'm doing okay. I'm just really tired of the routine.
How long have you been experiencing these worries and repeated checks about your design work?

How long? Gosh, um... you know, I’ve actually tried to figure that out myself, and I honestly don't know. I really couldn't give you a specific timeframe. 

Because the thing is, when you're a graphic designer—especially working at an agency where the standards are just incredibly high—you're basically trained from day one to be obsessed with the details. Even back when I was getting my bachelor's degree, my typography professors would absolutely drill us on things like kerning and leading and margin alignment. If your file wasn't pixel-perfect, you'd get torn apart in the class critique. So, checking my work, zooming in at 400% to make sure two lines align perfectly... I've *always* done that. That's just what makes you a good designer. It's expected of you.

But as for when it crossed the line from being just, you know, normal professional diligence into this exhausting, repetitive loop where I can't just export a file and be done with it? I have no idea. It's not like I woke up one morning and suddenly couldn't hit the "save" button without checking my clipping masks twenty times. It feels more like it just crept up on me incredibly slowly. 

Maybe I started double-checking the hex codes for a really demanding client, just to be safe. And then maybe that turned into triple-checking. And then, before I knew it, that just became my baseline for every single project, even if it's just a tiny, unimportant social media graphic that takes five minutes to build. I've sat at my desk and tried to trace it back to a specific project or a specific month, like, was it that massive rebrand we did for that beverage company? Was it when we got the new account director? But nothing really stands out as a clear starting point. 

So, yeah, I wish I could tell you, "Oh, it started exactly six months ago," but I really don't have a clue. It all just blends together. It's so hard to separate where my normal, detail-oriented work ethic ends and this frustrating new habit begins, you know? It just gradually became my new normal at the office, and I didn't even fully realize how much time it was eating up until I started missing those internal deadlines with Sarah that I told you about.
Are you concerned that your symptoms might be impacting your chances of getting promoted to a creative director role?

Yes, exactly. I mean, like I was touching on a few minutes ago, that is honestly my single biggest worry in all of this. Because, you know, strictly speaking, I am still getting my work done. At the end of the day, the clients get their finished files, the campaigns launch, and the agency gets paid. So from the outside, maybe it looks fine. 

But internally, behind the scenes, it is really taking a toll on my professional reputation. Missing those internal deadlines with my project manager, Sarah, is starting to become a pattern. And I hate that, because I have always prided myself on being reliable, but I just get so stuck checking everything that I have to push my drafts back a day or two. And people notice that. Management notices when you become the bottleneck in the workflow. 

And then, even worse than the deadlines, is what I mentioned about the actual designs. To be a creative director, you have to be the visionary. You have to be the one pushing the envelope and inspiring the junior designers. But I am actively holding back on my bolder design ideas. I will literally sketch out something really dynamic and complex, and then I will just scrap it and build something completely safe and minimalist instead. And I am doing that purely because I am so terrified that if I make a complex file with dozens of layers and effects, I will overlook something. I am so scared a layer will be accidentally hidden or a margin will be a millimeter off, and I will not catch it, and it will go to print with a glaring mistake. 

So I just dumb my own work down to make it easier to check. But by doing that, I feel like I am completely damaging my chances of moving toward a creative director role anyway. You do not promote someone who only pitches safe, boring concepts. You promote the innovator. So I am sitting at my desk, looking at my portfolio, knowing I have the talent to lead, but I am too paralyzed by the fear of missing a detail to actually show it. I am forty now, which is the exact time I should be stepping into agency leadership, and it just kills me to think I am sabotaging my own promotion because of this endless checking loop. It is just so incredibly frustrating to watch it happen and feel like I cannot stop it, you know?
Are there any situations or activities outside of your design work where you feel like you're checking or rehearsing things repeatedly, even if it's not directly related to your job?

Outside of work? Um... no, honestly, not really. I’ve actually thought about that, like, do I do this with locking my front door or checking to make sure the oven is off? And I don't. I'm completely fine at home. I lock the door once, I walk away, I don't even think twice about it. I don't rehearse conversations with my friends or anything like that, either. 

It really is entirely, one hundred percent focused on my design files. It’s like my brain only gets stuck in that loop when I’m sitting in front of Adobe Creative Suite. 

Like, just to give you a really clear picture of what the actual process looks like when I’m trying to wrap up a project... before I submit work now, I can't just hit export, attach it to an email, and be done with it. I will literally close the program, sit back, and then immediately re-open the file. And then I’ll sit there and compare the layers. I'll toggle the visibility on and off, on and off, looking at the background, the text layers, the vector shapes, just to make absolutely sure nothing shifted or got hidden by accident. And then I’ll re-save it. Sometimes I’ll save it as a new version, just to feel safe. 

And even after the file is finally sent off to Sarah or the client, my brain is still going. I’ll sit there and sometimes mentally walk through every single design choice one more time in my head. I'll just be staring at my monitor, thinking, "Okay, I set the drop shadow opacity to 40%, I checked the bleed on the left margin, I made sure the logo was perfectly centered..." I just rehearse the whole sequence of what I built to reassure myself that I didn't mess it up. 

And, you know, I want to be clear—because I don't want to make it sound worse than it is—it’s not like I’m sitting there doing this for eight hours straight. It doesn’t take over my whole day. I still go to my status meetings, I still grab coffee, I still function. But it does make me slower. It adds this heavy, tedious chunk of time to the end of every single task that just drags my productivity down. And, exactly like I was saying before about the promotions, it just makes me less free creatively. I'm so bogged down in the mechanical checking of the layers and the saving and the mental rehearsing that the actual art of it—the whole reason I became a designer in the first place—is just getting completely squeezed out. But yeah, outside of the agency? I don't do anything like this at all.
Are you feeling like your symptoms are significantly impacting your relationships or daily activities outside of the office?

Outside the office? Um... no, not really. Like I was saying just a minute ago, it really doesn't bleed into my personal life at all. My relationships with my friends, my family... my daily routine at home, all of that is totally fine. I don't check things around the house or obsess over my personal texts or anything like that. I can just exist normally when I'm not in front of my work computer.

But... gosh, it’s just so hard to let go of the work aspect of it, because that’s where the real impact is, and it just completely consumes my thoughts. Even when I'm at home on the weekends, I'm worrying about what's happening at the agency. Because, you know, technically, yes, I’m still getting my work done. The clients get their files, the campaigns go live, everything ships. But I just can't stop dwelling on the fact that I’ve started missing those internal deadlines. I know I mentioned Sarah earlier, but it just really, really weighs on me. It’s so unprofessional, and it’s entirely because I’m stuck in that endless checking loop. 

And then, honestly, the most heartbreaking part for me—and I know I’m repeating myself a bit here, but it's just so incredibly frustrating—is how I'm actively holding back on my bolder design ideas. I'll literally have a spark of inspiration for a really dynamic, multi-layered campaign, and I'll just kill it before it even makes it to the screen. I just get so paralyzed by the fear that if I build something complex, I’ll overlook something crucial. I’ll miss a hidden layer or a typo in a tiny font, and it’ll be a massive disaster. So I just play it safe. I water it down. 

And I know, I absolutely know, that doing this is completely damaging my chances of moving toward a creative director role. You can't lead a creative team if you're too terrified to take a creative risk. So, yeah, my personal life and relationships are intact, but professionally... I just feel like I'm completely sabotaging my own future because of this fear, and I just can't seem to turn it off.
Are you feeling like your symptoms are significantly affecting your overall quality of life or ability to function outside of your job as a graphic designer?

I know you're asking about outside of my job again, and I swear, I really am totally fine when I leave the building. My quality of life at home, my hobbies, all of that hasn't taken a hit at all. But... well, I guess the problem is that I just can't compartmentalize it, you know? 

Because even if I'm not physically checking things at home, my brain is just so stuck on the fallout of what's happening at the agency. I know I keep bringing it back to work, and I feel like a broken record here, but it’s just the absolute core of the issue for me. Because on paper, yes, I am still getting my work done. The final deliverables are going out, the clients are happy. But my ability to function *well*? To function like the senior designer I'm supposed to be? It's just shot. 

I've started missing those internal deadlines, which just completely goes against my work ethic, and worse than that... I'm just constantly holding back on my bolder design ideas. I’ll have these really great, innovative concepts, and I just squash them. I water them down to something basic because I am so deeply afraid that if I build a complex file, I’ll overlook something crucial and it'll go to print with an error. And the whole time I'm doing it, I'm just agonizing over the fact that I am actively damaging my chances of moving toward a creative director role. It’s like I’m watching myself ruin my own career progression in slow motion, and I'm the one doing it. 

So, sure, my ability to function outside of being a graphic designer is completely normal, but my life *as* a graphic designer—which is my whole passion, my whole livelihood—is just so compromised right now. I just can't seem to get past how much this fear is holding me back, even when I'm sitting on my couch at home on a Saturday. It just hangs over everything.
Are you feeling like your symptoms are significantly impacting your relationships or daily activities outside of the office?

I know we keep circling back to this, and I’m so sorry if I’m just sounding like a completely broken record here. I know you're asking about my personal life again, and I really am trying to answer that. My relationships are completely fine, honestly. I still go out to dinner with my friends, my family life is totally normal, I still do all my normal daily stuff around the house without any issues. 

But... it’s just that my brain never really leaves the agency, you know? Even when I'm out with friends or just trying to relax on a Sunday, I'm just sitting there agonizing over work. Because, yes, on paper, I’m still getting my work done. The final files are being delivered to the clients, the campaigns are launching. But behind the scenes, the way I'm working is just falling apart. I’ve started missing our internal deadlines, which I never, ever used to do, and it’s so embarrassing to have to explain to the project managers why a preliminary draft is a day and a half late just because I couldn't stop checking it. 

And... the part that just really breaks my heart, the thing that I just can't stop obsessing over even when I'm supposed to be enjoying my weekend, is how I'm constantly holding back on my bolder design ideas. Like, I’ll be out at a coffee shop, completely away from my desk, and I’ll get a flash of inspiration for this really vibrant, complex, multi-layered layout. And almost immediately, I just talk myself out of it. I tell myself, 'No, don't do that, it's too complicated, you're definitely going to overlook a hidden layer or forget to outline a tiny font and it'll go to print wrong.' So I just scrap it in my head before I even try. I go back on Monday and I pitch something incredibly safe and watered down. 

And I just know—I mean, I'm forty now, this is the time in my career where I really need to be stepping up and showing leadership—I know that by doing this, I am actively damaging my chances of moving toward a creative director role. You just can't get promoted to creative director if you're too terrified to pitch a bold idea. So, even though my personal relationships and my daily activities outside of work are totally fine, this intense fear of overlooking something is just bleeding into my headspace 24/7 and completely sabotaging my future. I just don't know how to break out of it.
Are you feeling like your symptoms are significantly impacting your ability to enjoy your free time or maintain your relationships with friends and family?

I... I feel like we’re just spinning our wheels on this one specific question, and I really don't mean to be difficult, I promise, but I genuinely don't know how else to explain it. I know you're trying to get a complete picture of my life outside the office, but like I've been saying, my relationships are totally fine. My family isn't upset with me, my friends still invite me to things, I still have free time on the weekends. 

But... *enjoying* that free time? That’s a completely different story. I can't really enjoy it. Because even if I'm physically sitting at a dinner party with my friends, mentally, I am just completely consumed by the mess I'm making at the agency. 

Because, like I keep trying to emphasize, even though I am technically still getting my work done and the clients are getting their final deliverables on time, the process behind it is just falling apart. I’m missing our internal deadlines now, which is just so incredibly unlike me, and it weighs on me the entire weekend. I'll be out at a movie or something, and all I can think about is how I had to ask the project manager for another extension on a draft. 

And then there's the actual creative side of it, which is the part that really haunts me when I'm supposed to be relaxing. I just can't stop agonizing over the fact that I am constantly holding back on my bolder design ideas. I get so terrified that if I actually execute a really complex, innovative concept, I’m going to overlook something critical in the file and it'll be a disaster. So I just play it safe. I water everything down.
